newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran leader urges vigilance, wargames to start.
newsitem.headline: Iran leader urges vigilance, wargames to start.

text.p: Iran's supreme leader on Tuesday urged Iranians to be vigilant against foreign threats as 200,000 elite troops prepared to launch wargames in the Gulf.
"Although there is no serious and real threat to our borders...we have to be vigilant," Ayatollah Ali Khamenei told thousands of people in the strategic Gulf port of Bandar Abbas.
"The moment, God forbid, the people and the youth of this country become careless that is the moment of danger," he said in remarks reported by state-run Tehran radio.

"Our government is based on popular support. Which world power can stand up to the Islamic Republic which is backed by millions of courageous and resistant people across our country?" Khamenei said after arriving in the port to watch the start on Tuesday evening of three days of amphibious military exercises.
Some 200,000 troops -- elite Revolutionary Guards units and paramilitary Basij volunteers -- were to take part in the wargames planned since last June, Iran's news agency IRNA said.
They would train for surprise attacks on "enemies" posing threats to the Islamic republic in the wargames which will stretch along the length of the Gulf and inland to western Iran.
Iran's southern coastline runs the length of the Gulf, through which about 15 million barrels of oil -- equal to Europe's daily consumption -- pass every day.

Khamenei said Iran would launch a "harsh response" against anyone threatening its security -- an apparent reference to reports that the United States might strike at the country if a link was established between Tehran and a bombing in June that killed 19 U.S. airmen in Saudi Arabia. Iran denies involvement.

Tehran radio said people chanting "Death to America" were marching to a desert region in central Iran to mark a failed U.S. military mission in April 1980 to free 52 Americans held hostage by Islamic militants at the U.S. embassy in Tehran.
The wargames will include major amphibious exercises in the Strait of Hormuz, conduit for half the world's oil exports.
Iranian media said Khamenei, commander-in-chief of Iran's half-million-strong armed forces, arrived in Bandar Abbas to a warm welcome from local officials and people.
Streets were decorated with banners, posters of Khamenei's predecessor, the Islamic republic's founder the late Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, the Iranian tricolour and coloured lights.

IRNA quoted Revolutionary Guards deputy commander, Brigadier General Rahim Safavi, as saying the exercises code-named "Tariq-ol Qods" (Road to Jerusalem) would include tests of surface-to-air, shore-to-sea and surface-to-surface missiles.

Khamenei said the United States and Israel had failed to isolate Iran and pledged that, despite their pressure, Tehran would be steadfast in its demand that "the Zionist regime (Israel) should get the hell out of Palestine", the radio said.

Safavi said Iran, which regularly holds wargames in the Gulf, wanted "to upgrade the quality of its personnel so that it can better defend Islamic ideals and safeguard territorial integrity", IRNA reported.

He said Iran would not allow any "alien power to destabilise regional security". Safavi said the departure of "intruding forces" -- a term often used to describe U.S. forces in the Gulf -- would help enhance cooperation among regional states.
In the Iranian capital, the Tehran Times newspaper called on Iran's Gulf Arab neighbours to increase cooperation and conclude a regional security pact encompassing all regional countries.

The six Arab oil states of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) -- Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, Oman and the United Arab Emirates -- have been wary of overtures from Iran, whose 60 million people outnumber them by more than two to one.

They have accused the Islamic republic of interfering in the internal affairs of GCC states and backed the UAE in its dispute with Iran over three islands near the entrance to the Gulf. Iran has denied the charges.
